subject_judgments.access_rationale: Law of Hostages (1799) is directly retrievable through Law of Hostages; its benchmark treatments on pages 371, 372, 382, 384 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The law allowed detention, fines, and property seizure against relatives of emigres or nobles in disturbed areas without proof of responsibility.

Life consulship and monarchical drift is directly retrievable through Consul for life; its benchmark treatments on pages 390 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Measures prepared in 1802 would extend Bonaparte's term and make him Consul for life, leaving France with an executive increasingly similar to a king.

Legislative opposition and purge of the Tribunate and Legislative Body is directly retrievable through legislative body; its benchmark treatments on pages 389, 390 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Experienced legislators used their limited functions to criticize treaties, special courts, Civil Code procedure, and the Concordat; Bonaparte used constitutional ambiguity and the Senate to remove eighty members.

Sieyès, Emmanuel-Joseph > Consulate and constitutional design, consuls supplies direct access to First Consul's supremacy and rejection of the Grand Elector on every frozen treatment page (377). The supported locators cover Bonaparte rejects a powerless Grand Elector and obtains overriding authority in the final executive structure.

Rule of law in ordinary life versus arbitrariness in high politics has usable access through rule of law on pages 384, 385, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 383, 390. Bonaparte cultivated regular laws, property rules, and safer administration for everyday life while repeatedly ignoring legal safeguards against political opponents and representative bodies.

Armed Neutrality, Copenhagen, and Anglo-Russian realignment is directly retrievable through Armed neutrality; its benchmark treatments on pages 380 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Paul I's alienation produced a Baltic league against British naval access, but Nelson's attack at Copenhagen and Paul's assassination reopened Anglo-Russian contacts.

Lists of notables and attenuated popular sovereignty has usable access through Sovereignty on pages 376, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 377. Citizens chose successive tenths for communal, departmental, and national lists, but the lists only identified eligibility and did not allow electors to choose officeholders directly.

Concordat of 1801 and the transformation of French Catholicism is directly retrievable through Concordat of 1801, Papacy; its benchmark treatments on pages 386, 387, 388, 389, 390, 398, 424 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Whole-book synthesis: The Concordat restored Catholic public life and hierarchy while accepting religious freedom, state financing, government nomination of bishops, clerical oaths, and the permanent property settlement.

Royalist restoration hopes and Louis XVIII's overture to Bonaparte has usable access through Louis XVIII on pages 382, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 381. Many monarchists hoped the First Consul would act as a French General Monck and restore the Bourbons after stabilizing France; Louis XVIII directly appealed to him.

No delivered heading provides a realistic first lookup for Political exhaustion, civic withdrawal, and peasant priorities; the benchmark requires treatment on page(s) 369. War losses, conscription, repeated political crises, and conflict over religion exhausted civic participation and made peace more urgent than regime activism.

décadi, Catholic Church > restoration and Concordat (1801-2), Concordat of 1801 supplies direct access to Sunday, the decadi, and restoration of public worship on every frozen treatment page (386, 389, 390). The supported locators cover The decadi requirement is dropped and official gestures toward Catholic mourning and worship prepare negotiations; The final abandonment of decadi for Sunday is counted among the settlement's welcome provisions; A solemn Easter mass at Notre-Dame publicly marks the restored Church and the perceived end of revolutionary conflict.

Battle of Novi and Joubert's death is directly retrievable through Novi, Battle of; its benchmark treatments on pages 372 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Joubert's death and the catastrophic defeat at Novi destroyed Sieyes's preferred military partner and intensified the emergency driving radical legislation and coup planning.

No delivered heading provides a realistic first lookup for Revolutionary war transformed Europe, but later expansion belonged to Napoleon's empire; the benchmark requires treatment on page(s) 381. Ten years of war transformed France and western Europe beyond the intentions of 1789 and produced enlarged borders and client territories.

bishops > under Concordat and Napoleonic settlement, Constitutional Church, refractory clergy > under the Concordat supplies direct access to Episcopal reset: constitutional and refractory churches on every frozen treatment page (387, 388). The supported locators cover Rival legitimate hierarchies and future appointment posed core obstacles to agreement; The Pope seeks resignations or deprives refractory bishops, the constitutional council is dismissed, and former constitutional clergy enter the new bench.

Treaty of Lunéville and postwar reopening has usable access through Lunéville, Treaty of on pages 379, 391, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 380. Lunéville entrenched France's continental gains and helped reopen postwar Europe to civilian travel and observation.

Lucien Bonaparte in the coup of Brumaire is directly retrievable through Bonaparte, Lucien, Brumaire, Coup of; its benchmark treatments on pages 374, 375 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. As president of the Five Hundred, Lucien helped arrange the transfer to Saint-Cloud and persuaded troops that Jacobins had attacked his brother, enabling military expulsion of the chamber.

Pius VI's death and mistaken expectations of Catholic collapse is directly retrievable through Pius VI; its benchmark treatments on pages 385, 386 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The death of captive Pius VI encouraged French anticlericals to imagine that the papacy and institutional Church were disappearing, an expectation quickly disproved by a new conclave and religious revival.

Bonaparte's consolidation of personal rule has usable access through consuls, Bonaparte, Napoleon > Consulate and reforms, Bonaparte, Napoleon > Rise to power and Brumaire coup on pages 374, 377, 390, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 383. Military prestige, constitutional supremacy, selective conciliation, repression, administrative reform, peace, and religious settlement progressively made the First Consul the indispensable guarantor of order.

Emigre return and preservation of confiscated property is directly retrievable through émigrés > amnesty and return of; its benchmark treatments on pages 383 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Emigres could return and receive amnesty if they accepted the permanent loss of property vested in the Republic, thereby separating personal reconciliation from restoration of the old social order.

Amiens, Peace of, Great Britain > peace negotiations and treaties supplies direct access to Peace of Amiens and postwar reopening on every frozen treatment page (380, 381, 390, 391). The supported locators cover British strategic and domestic circumstances lead to preliminary agreements in October 1801; The final terms, signed in March 1802, preserve French continental advantages and leave Britain only selected overseas acquisitions; News of Amiens frames the legislative passage and public celebration of the domestic religious settlement; Peace reopened continental travel and sent large numbers of British visitors to inspect a France previously known chiefly through wartime fear.

Concordat of 1801 supplies direct access to Church lands and the non-restoration settlement on every frozen treatment page (387, 388). The supported locators cover No church property sold since 1790 would be returned, and papal reservations about legality and Avignon are explicitly retained; The final settlement proceeds after both sides accept a completely new institutional beginning rather than old-regime restoration.

No delivered heading provides a realistic first lookup for Revolutionary gains and conditional popular support; the benchmark requires treatment on page(s) 369, 378. Rural attachment to equality, the end of seigneurial burdens and game rights, and ownership of national lands survived, but support depended on peace and predictable order.

Chouans (Chouannerie) > resurgence and suppression under Consulate supplies direct access to Pacification of chouannerie on every frozen treatment page (382, 383). The supported locators cover Most leaders accept peace after assurances on worship and hostage repeal, while holdouts are pursued; Cadoudal's agents are identified as the real perpetrators of the infernal-machine attack even though Jacobins bear the immediate repression.

Jourdan, Jean-Baptiste supplies direct access to Country in Danger motion (September 1799) on every frozen treatment page (373). The supported locators cover A substantial debate weighs renewed revolutionary mobilization against the constitutional danger of suspending normal procedure, and the motion loses clearly.

Forced loan on the rich (1799) has usable access through forced loan on the rich on pages 371, 384, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 372. The Jacobin-backed forced loan sought wartime revenue through punitive assessments on wealthy citizens after foreign occupation could no longer finance French armies.

The delivered headings do not implement the frozen lookup routes Kingdom of Naples and Consular recognition of Bourbon legitimacy, Naples, peace with France in 1801. Consequently page(s) 380 remain inaccessible for Kingdom of Naples and Consular recognition of Bourbon legitimacy: The Bourbon monarchy survives with recognized legitimacy while conceding territory and key-port garrisons to France.

Catholic Church > restoration and Concordat (1801-2), Concordat of 1801 supplies direct access to Bonaparte's instrumental and pragmatic use of religion on every frozen treatment page (385, 386). The supported locators cover Earlier restraint toward the Pope is introduced as evidence that Bonaparte did not underestimate the Church; His advice to treat religion like property, display of Islam in Egypt, and public case for religion as moral support reveal a consistent instrumental outlook.

Neo-Jacobin resurgence after Prairial has usable access through political clubs > Manège Club (Jacobin resurgence 1799) on pages 371, 372, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 373. Prairial reopened Jacobin newspapers, clubs, offices, and legislative influence, producing emergency measures reminiscent of Year II before a coordinated backlash halted the movement.

Prefects and administrative centralization is directly retrievable through Prefects; its benchmark treatments on pages 384 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Prefects replaced weaker directorial commissioners and linked central authority to departments through powers compared with, but broader than, old-regime intendants.

Organic Articles, Gallican controls, and the papal-authority paradox is directly retrievable through Gallicanism, Law on Cults (18 Germinal, Year X); its benchmark treatments on pages 388, 389 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Organic Articles unilaterally restricted papal communication and revived Gallican teachings even as the Concordat restored hierarchy and gave the papacy unprecedented authority over French bishops.

Royalists > social and regional support, Toulouse supplies direct access to Royalist insurrection in south-western France (1799) on every frozen treatment page (372, 373). The supported locators cover Renewed internal insurrection follows coalition landings and military reverses; The source describes the ten-thousand-strong rising, month of civil war, failure to take Toulouse, and collapse of supporting disturbances.

For Suppression of the 1799 Jacobin resurgence, political clubs > Manège Club (Jacobin resurgence 1799) retrieves page(s) 372: Official warnings, hostile publicity, eviction and final closure of the Manege Club, and rejection of indictments curb the movement. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 373, where the benchmark records Rejection of emergency rule and renewed battlefield success leave the anti-Jacobin Directory politically stronger.

French continental hegemony and pragmatic client settlement has usable access through Sister republics on pages 379, 381, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 380. By 1801 France controlled expanded frontiers and a belt of client territories while accommodating Bourbons in Etruria and Naples and extracting Louisiana from Spain.

Senate as conservative constitutional power is directly retrievable through Constitution of the Year VIII, Senate (French); its benchmark treatments on pages 377, 390 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Senate selected legislators from the national list and embodied Sieyes's long-standing idea of a body that would guard legality, though its powers were left obscure.

Brumaire, Coup of supplies direct access to Coup of Brumaire (18-19 Brumaire, Year VIII) on every frozen treatment page (374, 375). The supported locators cover Sieyes and Bonaparte coordinate with Lucien, Fouche, and Talleyrand and frame the operation as protection against Jacobin conspiracy; Directory resignations, Bonaparte's hostile reception, military clearing of the Five Hundred, and votes by a compliant quorum establish a provisional Consulate.

Manege Club is directly retrievable through Manège Club, political clubs > Manège Club (Jacobin resurgence 1799); its benchmark treatments on pages 371, 372 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The revived Jacobin club gathered veterans and deputies in the former Convention hall, becoming the most visible institutional focus of the 1799 left before eviction and closure.

No delivered heading provides a realistic first lookup for April 1802 celebrations as the burial of the Revolution; the benchmark requires treatment on page(s) 390. Peace, the defeat of visible political opposition, and restored Catholic worship converged in an Easter celebration presented as a new beginning and the public burial of revolutionary turmoil.

Elections of Year VII (1799) is directly retrievable through Elections of 1799; its benchmark treatments on pages 369, 370 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Directory again tried to manage electoral outcomes, but low turnout, split assemblies, anti-directorial deputies, and Jacobin gains produced a legislature willing to resist the executive.

Catholic Church > quarrel with the Revolution, Catholic Church > restoration and Concordat (1801-2), Concordat of 1801 supplies direct access to Revolutionary religious conflict and Catholic revival on every frozen treatment page (385, 386, 390). The supported locators cover Religious division is described as the deepest unresolved wound, despite official claims that the Church was disappearing; The election of Pius VII and Bonaparte's conciliatory signals demonstrate institutional resilience and a route to compromise; Restored public worship becomes one of the settlements celebrated as the Revolution's burial.

Kingdom of Etruria and Bourbon accommodation has usable access through Etruria, Kingdom of on pages 379, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 380. French-backed creation of a Bourbon kingdom in Tuscany showed that the Consular settlement could employ monarchy and legitimacy when strategically useful.

Royalist and Jacobin limits of constitutional opposition is directly retrievable through Royalists > constitutional and electoral politics; its benchmark treatments on pages 376, 377 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Both royalists and Jacobins sometimes adopted constitutional tactics, yet neither convincingly accepted compromise, the legitimacy of opponents, or permanent pluralism.

Fouche: police power and political control has usable access through Fouché, Joseph on pages 372, 383, 387, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 374. Fouche closed the Manege Club, participated in Brumaire, monitored Jacobins, identified royalist bombers, executed Bonaparte's anti-Jacobin purge, and later resisted aspects of church reconciliation.

Pius VII and the possibility of papal compromise is directly retrievable through Pius VII; its benchmark treatments on pages 386, 387, 388 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Pius VII's earlier claim that Christianity could coexist with democracy and equality made him a plausible partner for France's pragmatic ruler.

Security of national lands and the revolutionary property settlement has usable access through émigrés > property of (national lands) on pages 383, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 369, 385, 387. The Consulate protected land and property transfers made during the Revolution against emigre or church restitution, making new ownership a durable basis of the regime.

The Revolution declared over: stability purchased by sacrificing 1789 principles has usable access through Consulate on pages 378, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 381, 390. The Consulate claimed to complete and preserve the Revolution, but durable stability required surrender of most political principles associated with 1789.

For Brigandage and special criminal courts, special criminal courts retrieves page(s) 384: Conscription fugitives, royalist gangs, and criminal bands overwhelm local order while troops remain at the front. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 385, where the benchmark records Peace permits troop deployment and special courts against brigandage, allowing disorder to subside.

Disintegration of the Second Coalition is directly retrievable through Austria > military campaigns and coalitions, Paul I (Tsar of Russia); its benchmark treatments on pages 378, 379, 380 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Austrian pursuit of separate territorial aims, Russian resentment, failed operations in Holland and Switzerland, and Paul I's withdrawal dissolved the coalition advantage.

Great Britain > peace negotiations and treaties supplies direct access to British war-weariness and the opening to peace on every frozen treatment page (380, 381). The supported locators cover Domestic discontent, the Irish question, Pitt's resignation, and Addington's peace feelers are linked to France's renewed continental control; English jubilation over preliminaries suppresses criticism of terms favourable to France.

Civil Code: preparation and property ordering is directly retrievable through Civil Code; its benchmark treatments on pages 385, 389 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Bonaparte drove a long-delayed codification project, personally participating in drafting a clear framework for holding and transferring property.

Party politics, factions, and the general will is directly retrievable through general will; its benchmark treatments on pages 376 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Directorial republicans treated organized political groups as illegitimate factions because they assumed a single honest general will, and they failed to build an organized moderate centre.

Military crisis and recovery in 1799 has usable access through Novi, Battle of, Batavian Republic on pages 372, 373, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 370. Defeats in Italy, threatened invasion, Joubert's death, Novi, and landings in Holland drove political emergency before victories in the Batavian and Helvetic republics restored confidence.

Chouans (Chouannerie) > resurgence and suppression under Consulate supplies direct access to Renewed chouannerie in autumn 1799 on every frozen treatment page (374). The supported locators cover Chouan bands renew royalist action, occupy Le Mans and other cities, and expose the Directory's inability to control either extreme.

Directory—instability, political practice, and collapse has usable access through directory, Constitution of the Year III (1795), Constitution of the Year VIII on pages 369, 375, 376, 377, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 370. The Directory's repeated manipulation of elections, dependence on force, factional conflict, and inability to establish legitimate stable practice culminated in its collapse, even though constitutional design alone did not make failure inevitable.

Marengo, Battle of, Hohenlinden, Battle of supplies direct access to Campaigns of 1800: Marengo and Hohenlinden on every frozen treatment page (379). The supported locators cover The source narrates the secret Alpine crossing, near-disaster at Marengo, Austrian armistice, and Moreau's later knockout blow in Germany.

Constitution of the Year VIII is directly retrievable through Constitution of the Year VIII, Consulate; its benchmark treatments on pages 377, 378 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The new constitution preserved nominal suffrage and multiple institutions while monopolizing legislative initiative in the government and placing overriding authority in the First Consul.

Plebiscite of 1800 supplies direct access to Plebiscite on the Constitution of Year VIII on every frozen treatment page (378). The supported locators cover The reported millions in favour are contrasted with mass abstention, manipulation, and implementation before counting was complete.

Law on Cults of 18 Germinal, Year X has usable access through Law on Cults (18 Germinal, Year X) on pages 389, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 390. French law promulgated the Concordat together with the unilateral Organic Articles, making religious reconciliation inseparable from state restrictions on the Church.

Malta, Great Britain > peace negotiations and treaties supplies direct access to War with Britain: Egypt, Malta, and maritime limits on every frozen treatment page (380, 381). The supported locators cover British squadrons isolate Egypt, British forces compel surrender, and Malta falls, demonstrating the limits of French reach at sea; Amiens leaves Britain selected colonial gains while it tacitly accepts French continental changes.

Tribunate, Legislative Body, and Council of State is directly retrievable through Tribunate; its benchmark treatments on pages 377, 389 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Tribunate could debate but not vote, the Legislative Body could vote but not debate, neither could initiate laws, and government proposals were drafted through a revived Council of State.

No delivered heading provides a realistic first lookup for Depoliticization, disappearance of the independent press, and public preference for stability; the benchmark requires treatment on page(s) 390. By 1802 independent press and representative debate had largely disappeared, while police reports suggested public contempt for legislators and concern centred on Bonaparte's safety.

Financial stabilization under the Consulate is directly retrievable through Bank of France; its benchmark treatments on pages 384 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Bank of France, reliable cash payment of state debts, stronger tax collection, restored public credit, and a claimed balanced budget made fiscal authority appear regular and responsible.

Bonaparte, Napoleon > Rise to power and Brumaire coup supplies direct access to Bonaparte's return from Egypt and cross-party appeal on every frozen treatment page (374). The supported locators cover Triumphal receptions and a reputation for victory make Bonaparte the available general around whom multiple factions gather.

Sieyès, Emmanuel-Joseph > Directory and Coup of Brumaire, Sieyès, Emmanuel-Joseph > Consulate and constitutional design, Bonaparte, Napoleon > Rise to power and Brumaire coup supplies direct access to Bonaparte and Sieyes: rival designs for executive power on every frozen treatment page (375, 377). The supported locators cover Bonaparte's case for an expansive executive is contrasted with Sieyes's continuing Enlightened fear of despotism; Bonaparte rejects the ceremonial Grand Elector and secures overriding authority for the First Consul.

Sieyès, Emmanuel-Joseph > Directory and Coup of Brumaire, Sieyès, Emmanuel-Joseph > Consulate and constitutional design supplies direct access to Sieyes: constitutional strategy and executive concentration on every frozen treatment page (370, 371, 374, 377). The supported locators cover Sieyes accepts a directorial seat because he judges the moment ripe for constitutional change; Prairial places effective executive power in his hands even though the legislature believes it has prevailed; He concludes that only a military-backed coup can strengthen the executive and recruits Bonaparte after other generals prove unavailable or reluctant; Several Year VIII institutions embody his ideas, while Bonaparte defeats his proposed design for the executive.

Concordat of 1801 supplies direct access to Religious freedom and a state-controlled Catholic majority church on every frozen treatment page (387, 388). The supported locators cover The first article preserves freedom of belief while public funding and governmental appointment make the restored Church a state institution; Bishops become clerical counterparts of prefects within an organization aligned to state geography.

Reconciliation of middle classes and property holders has usable access through Consulate on pages 384, but the delivered index does not retrieve the benchmark treatment on page(s) 383. The Consulate sought elite and middle-class allegiance by crushing levelling politics, repealing coercive fiscal measures, guaranteeing property, paying creditors, and offering visible order.

Coup of Prairial (June 1799) is directly retrievable through Prairial, Coup of; its benchmark treatments on pages 370, 371 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. The Councils forced Treilhard, La Revelliere, and Merlin from the Directory and installed replacements, producing the only legislative purge of the executive under the Year III constitution.

Bank of France is directly retrievable through Bank of France; its benchmark treatments on pages 384 are all supported by the canonical locator audits. Creation of the Bank of France signalled a decisive break with long revolutionary distrust of banking and supported restored public credit.

For Infernal-machine attack and the purge of Jacobins, Infernal Machine Plot (1800), Seychelles, Guiana retrieves page(s) 383: The bombing, royalist authorship, deliberate misattribution, executions, shootings, and mass deportations are set out together. No supported locator under those subject-aligned headings reaches page(s) 384, where the benchmark records Bonaparte explicitly treats exemplary repression as a means of reconciling the middle classes to his Republic.

Louisiana supplies direct access to Louisiana cession and pressure on Spain on every frozen treatment page (380). The supported locators cover Spain cedes the vast Louisiana territory as the price of hoped-for influence in the French-directed Italian settlement.
